Introduction & Executive Summary** ###### **1.1 Introduction** Soon after the release of the previous edition of our 3-Year Copper Forecast, the sovereign debt crisis, which began a few months prior as an isolated Greek problem, apparently spread across a number of Eurozone countries. Throughout May and in the first couple of weeks of June, risk aversion rocketed, on the back of concerns over the likelihood that other highly indebted economies, such as Spain and Portugal, could follow Greece’s suit. Added to these fears were the emergence of economic data that painted a lacklustre picture for industrial commodity demand in the United States as well as continued concerns over the prospects for Chinese growth to slow in the not too distant future. Investors reaction to the above saw copper prices continue to trend downwards. Although they found support at around $6,500/tonne in mid-May and for the next few days actually recovered, these gains were soon wiped out, as prices collapsed to less than $6,100/ tonne in early June, marking a record low for the yearto-date. From that point onwards and through to late July, prices moved sideways, mostly trading within a $6,400-6,800/ tonne range, as any calm the markets received from a series of relatively positive signals on the European sovereign debt front were countered by disappointing developments in the US and, to a lesser extent, Chinese economies. The tables were turned by a series of positive developments in the global economy, which spurred a return of investors to industrial commodities. Before the end of July, copper had broken through the $7,000/ tonne barrier and, during the better part of August, prices have traded in a $7,200-7,450/tonne range. We would stress that, in spite of this improvement in sentiment, the market has over the last few weeks continued to be shadowed by considerable uncertainty towards the outlook for global economic growth and industrial production. Such issues were instrumental in averting further price gains and, as a very recent correction to just over $7,000 illustrates, perpetuating risks to the downside. Looking at copper’s apparent fundamentals over the last few months, these have continued to improve from a weak base. Although we believe that the market remained in surplus during the period, it seems to us that the size of the excess supply was declining. As we discuss in the outlook section of this chapter, this trend has been key in our revision of our supply-demand projections. These now see the copper market turn to a slight deficit from as early as the third quarter of

this year. Reported inventories have trended downwards since our previous 3-Year Copper Forecast was published, with LME stocks in late August hovering at around 400,000 tonnes, compared to nearly 500,000 tonnes at end-April and around 555,000 tonnes at their peak in February. Reported stocks in China have also been falling, with Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks amounting to 110,000 tonnes in late August, compared to 189,000 tonnes at end-April. Offsetting these declines, we would expect unreported inventories in China to have continued growing, although, in line with dwindling surpluses, net inflows are likely to have stopped recently. Looking ahead, we maintain a mildly positive outlook for copper’s fundamentals over the rest of this year. Although to-date consumption growth has been limited, we have been positively surprised by some of the news relating to some major mature markets’ players. Moreover, we continue to project an acceleration in the final four months of the year, fuelled by consumer inventory replenishment, as discussed in more detail later in this chapter. Although continued growth in production will offset a part of these gains, we expect that the market will to see a substantial deficit in the final quarter of the year. The above is far from suggestive of a major tightness in the copper market. Indeed, the fuel for the rally we forecast for the final quarter of the year is expected to, once again, come from investors buying into the positive medium to longer-term outlook of the copper market and as such once again “bringing forward” the price effect. As such, we continue to expect prices will once again breach the $8,000/tonne mark before the end of the year, although we now expect that prices will not be able to stay above that level for long before retracing. “lost” over the period. A close examination of the monthly reported consumption (defined as apparent consumption plus net changes in SHFE stocks) against semis production data and net scrap imports has illustrated that most of these additions to unreported stockpiles probably took place in the first quarter and that their monthly volume has been declining. We specifically looked at the difference between reported consumption and semis production and compared that with net scrap imports. This illustrated that the “gap” between semis production and reported consumpt

ion has been rising in recent months, while net scrap imports have been moving sideways, suggesting a tightening market within the country. Moving into 2011, we expect copper’s fundamentals to suffer a temporary set back. In the first quarter, seasonal quarter-on-quarter declines (related to the Chinese new year) are forecast for both production and consumption, but the one for the latter is augmented by the re-stocking cycle coming to an end, as well as temporary weakness in mature economies’ growth, as discussed in the Chapter 2. The latter weakness is expected to be carried into the second quarter, when we see a brief return to surplus, before the market tightens once again later in the year. Later in the year, in contrast, we would be surprised if the $8,000/tonne mark were not comfortably and sustainably breached. In the final year of the forecast period we see the gap between demand and supply widen further. Coupled with ongoing demand by investors, who are unlikely to leave the commodities complex any time soon, this sees prices average above $8,000/tonne in 2012. ###### **1.2 Economic Assumptions** GFMS’ view on how the global macroeconomic backdrop will develop over the forecast period holds paramount importance for our projections for copper supply, demand and prices. Given the ongoing uncertainty in the economic and financial markets, GFMS highlight our economic assumptions in three different, probability weighted scenarios. It is worth presenting the key assumptions of our three scenarios, which are discussed in detail in Chapter 2. both North America and Europe.

Moving to China and other emerging markets, as authorities move to rein in surging inflation, a slow-down is likely to emerge there too. As such, we have revised downwards our projections for global GDP growth to 2.1% next year. A marginal acceleration is expected in the final year of the forecast period, as more traditional sources of growth (for instance, consumer spending) start to improve, aided by unemployment beginning to recede in some of the large mature economies. **Scenario B:** (with a 20% probability outcome). The increasingly unlikely (hence our scaling back of the probability we have ascribed to it) bullish alternative scenario sees global GDP growth this year reaching 3.9%, with only a modest slow-down to an average 3.5% per annum over 2011-2012. These figures are premised on a perpetuation of ultra-lose monetary policy in mature economies, which sees healthy growth despite underlying problems, at the expense of higher levels of inflation. In China, authorities are expected to continue their pro-growth policy and average GDP growth over the three years stays above 10%. **Base Case Scenario:** (with a 50% probability outcome). We have revised upwards the majority of our 2010 GDP growth projections under this scenario since the previous edition of the 3-Year Copper Forecast and we now expect the global economy to grow by 3.3% (compared to 2.9% previously). In contrast, our forecast for 2011 growth has been scaled down, as we are increasingly concerned about the indebtedness of governments and the world economy’s overreliance on stimulus packages over the last twelve months. As the artificial stimuli begin to be withdrawn and credit accessibility worsens, GDP growth is likely to slow in **Scenario C:** (with a 30% probability outcome). The flipside to the above variant sees the sovereign balance sheet rebuild materially affect growth, particularly next year, when global GDP growth is forecast to fall to 1.5% and advanced economies’ industrial production growth turn negative. An improvement is then forecast for the final year of the forecast period, although even this is modest, with global GDP increasing by just 2.2%, compared to an average rate of 3.5% during the last decade. ###### **1.3 The Dollar** The US dollar was perhaps the biggest winner, at least for a short period, from the European sovereign debt crisis. The greenback benefited both from the explosion in risk aversion and the “flight to quality” this triggered, but also from the pressure on the common European currency, as investors lost confidence in both many of the underlying economies’ fundamentals but also the currency’s very viability, this due to the apparent lack of common ground among key members of the Eurozone. As a result, the dollar:euro rate continued to fall after the release of the previous edition of our 3- Year Forecast, in early May falling through $1.30 and reaching the low-$1.20s later in the month. Towards the end of the month, adding to the currency’s sovereign debt woes, sentiment towards economic growth in the United States and China took a hit from a series of uninspiring economic indicators, boosting risk aversion. In early June the rate fell through $1.20, for the first time since March 2006. A partial restoration of confidence in the ability of the Eurozone to pull through and some positive news on the global economic front have seen a recovery since then and from midJuly through to the present time, the rate has traded between $1.26 and $1.33. We continue to see the euro recovering against the US currency later in the year under our **Base Case** , but we have decided to revise our projections to show a more modest recovery from the current upper 1.20s. As such, although our projected full-year average rate of 1.33 remains higher than the year-to-date average, it is considerably lower than the 1.38 projection featured in the previous edition of this report. Our medium to longer-term expectations remain broadly unchanged and see a cyclical recovery of the greenback against the euro, as US interest rates rise from their current nearzero levels, that will see the exchange rate average 1.20 in 2012. Our bullish **Scenario B** sees the dollar weaken throughout the forecast period, as risk aversion evaporates in light of the strong recovery in global markets and higher US inflation that are assumed under this scenario. By the final year of the forecast period, we expect a return to the 2008 peak (on an annual average basis), of 1.46. In contrast, the bleak state of global markets sees a slow but steady advancement of the greenback against the common currency under **Scenario C** . By 2012 an average of 1.18 rate is forecast for the full year. It is worth also adding that, over the last couple months, we have often noted a negative correlation between sentiment towards the outlook for the US economy and the strength of the greenback. In the case of copper, where the overwhelming bulk of activity is essentially unreported, the task becomes ever more difficult. Nevertheless, using what limited data is available and combining that with anecdotal information, which we obtain through field research, conclusions on the direction and relevance of investor activity in copper can be reached. The copper price fluctuations since the eruption of the sovereign debt crisis have been undoubtedly fuelled in the main by investor activity. The fundamental market continues to mainly play a secondary role of giving signals to speculators and strategic players alike. The graph at the bottom right of this page features weekly investor positions in copper futures listed on the Comex exchange. The figures are calculated using the disaggregated open interest data distributed by the CFTC and includes aggregated net positions for all classes of trading institutions/individuals reported on, excluding “Producer/Merchant/Processor/User”. As can be seen in the chart, the aggregate net long (which is understood to proxy investor positions on the exchange) fell from around 680,000 tonnes at the end of April to a low of 463,000 tonnes in early July. From that point onwards, positions recovered, to 678,000 tonnes on 10th August, although we would be surprised if by now they were not considerably lower. It is worth noting that activity in Comex copper futures comprises the smaller part of global investment in copper, with the balance taking place in LME futures, on which disaggregated data on investor and commercial (relating to consumer and producer hedging) positions is not available. Elsewhere, the general themes we discussed in detail in the previous edition of our 3-Year Forecast remain relevant to the copper market through to the present time. Specifically, we continue to expect a strong investor presence in the market, even though we appreciate that the excitement that was in place last year towards industrial commodities may have subsided somewhat, as investors believe the bulk of potential gains have already been realised. Elsewhere, we continue to expect further inflows into commodity indic

es and that this will remain supportive for copper investment (as most mainstream indices, including the GSCI and DJ-UBSCI, contain some copper). The chart on page 8 features quarterly CFTC reports on fund investment in commodity index products since the end of 2007. As we have often noted, the bulk of copper investment activity forms part of a wider commodity strategy with only a small niche of investors being specifically interested in the red metal. As a result of this, copper prices often show relatively strong correlations with other commodity prices. This is illustrated in the graph below which features rolling 20-day correlation coefficients between copper prices and the Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI) as well as the DowJones UBS Commodity Index (DJ-UBSCI). It is worth stressing nevertheless that, given the nature of speculative investment, even during these times noteworthy corrections (albeit perhaps short-lived) are likely to take place. The strong involvement of investors in the copper market is expected to continue into the final year of the forecast period and most probably also beyond. Indeed, we cannot see how prices could reach our projected peak above $9,000/tonne in that year and the annual average of $8,100/tonne, were it not for positive investor interest in the metal. It is finally worth adding an update to the copper physical fund that ScotiaMocatta filed for last summer and has been trying to get off the ground since. The latest information suggests that, due to a lack of sufficient interest by investors, the bank has decided to abandon the product, even though regulatory approval had been attained. ###### **1.5 Consumption** We have revised our estimates and projections for global copper consumption in 2010 upwards somewhat since the previous issue of our 3-Year Quarterly Forecast, as a strong recovery in the mature economies particularly over the opening months of the year coupled with healthy consumption in China, has seen impressive demand growth over the first half of the year. We now expect global consumption to grow by 8.0% to 18.877 million tonnes, up from the 7.6% growth reported in our last forecast. Reflecting the above, the quarterly breakdown of demand over the remaining part of 2010 sees consumption continuing on an upward trend. After a seasonal drop in the third quarter, we expect growth (on a quarter-on-quarter basis) to pick up again in the fourth quarter to 4.0%. Many headwinds remain over the short, and indeed medium to longer term, as a result of concerns that rising levels of government spending that have been implemented in an effort to kick-start economic growth will, inherently, need to be reined in. Whilst we are already seeing signs of this, our Base Case scenario sees this trend intensifying over 2011 year and, with the underlying economic environment remaining fragile, we may observe a subsequent slowing of economic growth in a number of key markets. The impact on copper consumption will be particularly noticeable in the mature economies, where we are also likely to see winding down of consumer restocking next year. However, even China will not be immune

as the government steps up efforts to cool the economy following the breakneck expansion that has been seen recently. **8** Independent - Informed - International 3-Year Copper Forecast - August 2010 **CONFIDENTIAL** Following 3.3% growth in 2011, GFMS see global copper demand picking up in 2012, recording an increase of 4.1% to 20.312 million tonnes. However, given the debt legacy in the mature economies and that we expect to see a continuation of the trends discussed in section 3.1, the engines of copper consumption growth will remain the BRICs and other emerging countries. ###### **1.6 Production** We have made significant revisions to our projections for mine production during the 2010-2012 period. This has been the result of a detailed bottom-up review of those projects where we had expected growth to emerge. In many cases, the latest information available suggests that the production targets that our past forecasts had been based on are proving too optimistic. As such, although we continue to project above-trend growth throughout 2010-2012, this is far more contained than we had originally envisaged, averaging 2.5% per annum during the forecast period. As far as the sources of this growth are concerned, we continue to expect the rise in annual mine production through to 2012 to almost exclusively come from Africa and Latin America. Within the former, growth is expected in both Zambia and, to a lesser extent, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). In Latin America, after being more or less flat year-on-year in 2010, production in both Chile and Peru is expected to post material increases next year and in 2012. Considering the breakdown of production growth by extraction technology, we continue to forecast solvent extraction electrowinning (SX-EW) rising faster than concentrate production, with average annual growth rates for the two forecast at 3.5% and 2.3% respectively. The acceleration of mine production that we project for the 2010-2012 period will be reflected in a similar increase in refined production. Specifically, we expect global cathode production to rise by 2.6% this year, boosted further by the rise in scrap availability, itself the result of higher price levels. Yet stronger increases of 3.0% and 2.9% are expected to take place next year and in 2012, as mine output growth accelerates further. By the final year of the forecast period, global refined production is expected to reach 19.987 million tonnes, compared to 18.377 million tonnes last year. It is worth adding here that we continue to believe that, throughout the forecast period, smelting and refining capacity will remain more than sufficient to process material coming out of the ground as well as scrap. |

###### **1.7 Market Outlook** ###### **Base Case Scenario** Looking at the table below, featuring our quarterly estimates and projections for supply and demand through to the end of next year, the most obvious revision to our projections since the previous edition of our 3-Year Copper Forecast is the fact that we now see the market turn to deficit (albeit only at the margin) from as early as the third quarter of this year, with a deficit exceeding 100,000 tonnes emerging in the last three months of 2010. This reflects a significantly lower refined production forecast for the second half of the year, against virtually unchanged consumption forecasts for the period. The revision of our global refined production estimate reflects our understanding that mine production growth in the second half of the year seems set to fall considerably short of what we had expected, as a number of projects and operations are failing to meet targets, while output from others continues its secular decline. Against this, consumption seems to continue to grow, both in mature economies as well as in China and other emerging markets. The changes to our quarterly figures also see the overall balance for 2010 turn negative, although allowing for a reasonable margin of error, the 28,000 tonne deficit we forecast should be interpreted as a virtually balanced market. Moreover, as we noted earlier in this chapter, we believe that the principal driver of copper price movements has been and will remain investor activity in the metal. As such, contrasting

the improvement in our outlook for the market’s supply-demand fundamentals, we have actually revised our price outlook downwards, taking into consideration the events that unfolded in the last few months as well as our assessment of the current sentiment in the market. Although we continue to see investor buying driving prices through the $8,000/ tonne mark before the end of the year, we are no longer convinced the venture above that level will be sustainable. Moving to 2011, the slow-down we forecast for the global economy in the first half of the year sees copper’s supply-demand fundamentals take a hit and the market return to balance overall over the period, with parts of the second quarter in fact probably moving into surplus. In part reacting to this but also due to the rise in risk aversion we expect will emerge during the period, investors are likely to liquidate some of the long positions accrued in the final quarter of 2010. The drag from balance sheet rebuilding pushes down growth rates across a host of economies in **Scenario C** . That said, partly due to results so far this year we have revised up our 2010 growth projections under this scenario, and global GDP growth therefore still reaches 2.7%. A factor contributing to this slowdown is the absence of quantitative easing in the **United States** .  Also impeding growth from exporters in the United States under this scenario is the fact that the US dollar appreciates to an average of $1.23/€ in 2011 and to $1.18/€ in 20

12.  As a result of these factors, US GDP is anticipated to grow by a mere 0.5% in 2011, before a slight improvement to 1.1% in 2012.

Given the difficulties faced by the **Japanese** economy over the past 20 years and its export driven nature, it is unsurprising that it struggles to avoid an outright return to recession under Scenario C.  Therefore, GDP is forecast to grow by just 0.3% in 2011, before accelerating somewhat in the final year of the forecast. 

Countries that are more reliant on domestic growth during this period will perform better and, given the industrialisation taking place in many developing countries, they will continue to be the best performers. Needless to say **Chinese** growth will be strongest, although by its stellar standards an average growth of 8.7% in the next three years will represent a fair dip. Meanwhile, **India** also experiences strong growth, at an average rate of 6.6% over the forecast period.

###### **3.1 Historical Trends** 

A constant theme of our analysis is the relatively low rate of copper consumption growth over the 19992009 period, with GFMS estimates showing the average annual growth rate over the period at just 2.2% per annum.  This is one of the lowest rates for all of the base metals and, importantly, reflects substitution and miniaturisation issues that have affected copper consumption due to high prices and competition from aluminium and plastics in particular. 

Following the “dot.com” bubble in 2000, when copper consumption in the mature economies peaked at 8.935 million tonnes, and in the aftermath of the 9- 11 terrorist attacks in the United States, the mature economies in the Western World suffered a huge loss of confidence.  The authorities’ solution was to flood the market with liquidity and to slash interest rates.  This provided the foundations for one of the strongest bull markets across numerous asset classes, that started in 2003 and ran until 2008.  As we have discussed in earlier reports, this boost to liquidity came against a background of tight copper supply and it was this, rather than strong demand growth, that underpinned the bull market in prices. 

This explosion of liquidity fuelled strong growth in consumption spending in mature economies

Asian production increased at an average annual rate of 7.0% over 1999-2009, driven by strong growth in Chinese production.  The region overtook the Americas in 2005 as the largest producing copper region and last year it accounted for 44% of the global total.  Being a natural consequence of the dramatically higher base, we expect production growth in this region to slow over 2010-2012, to an average annual rate of 3.0%.  Nevertheless, this will amount to an increase of 762,000 tonnes in the region’s annual production over the three year period, equivalent to 47% of the increase in global production.  China alone is expected to see growth of a little less than half a million tonnes in its annual production over the three years. 

As we noted earlier, **China** has been the principal driver of growth in Asian refined production over the last decade and this was also the case in 2009, when output 

from the country grew by 8.6% to 4.121 million tonnes. After a lacklustre start to the year, refined production strengthened over the second half of 2009 in line with a recovery in scrap availability, a factor which had previously served to restrict production.  This rising trend in the country’s refined output has continued into 2010, with official data suggesting output over the first six months rose by 17.7% year-on-year to 2.257 million tonnes. 

Going forward we expect capacity in the country will continue to grow.  Jiangxi Copper is said to have met its 800,000 tonne per year target in 2009, and is looking at lifting production to 900,000 tonnes in 2010.  This year will also see production boosted by the expansion of Tongling’s Jinlong plant to 350,000 tonnes per year and Yunnan’s ongoing expansion at its Baoding refinery, which is expected to reach capacity of 200,000 tpy in 2011.  In addition, Xiangguang Copper Co is also looking to boost production to 600,000 tonnes per year by mid-2011 from its current 200,000 tonne per year capacity. ###### **Africa** 

Production in Africa grew strongly over the 1999-2009 period, increasing at an average annual rate of 5.2%. However, last year saw diverse performance in the region as the DRC saw strong expansion in line with the start up of Tenke Fungurume, whereas Zambian production suffered in line with the global economic downturn.  Going forward, we expect significant growth in Africa in line with increases in SX-EW production in particular, forecasting cumulative growth of 51% over the forecast period to over one million tonnes in 2012.

###### **Oceania** 

GFMS are expecting refined production in **Oceania** to dip by 4.6% this year due to falling grades at certain operations and given the loss of output at Olympic Dam earlier in the year. At 500,000 tonnes in 2012, production from the Oceania region will be virtually identical to the 2008 figure. 

###### **Europe** 

The latest revisions to the ICSG’s data suggest that European refined production fell by 1.3% last year, compared to previous estimates of a drop in excess of 4%.  The revision largely related to new data suggesting that Russian production rose instead of declined year-on-year. 

Naturally, given a lack of material drop last year, our projections for growth going forward are far more limited than in our previous Quarterly.  The only major project expected to come on stream is the Las Cruces operation in **Spain** .  Las Cruces’ SX-EW operation is due to reach full 72,000 tonnes by 2011, even though, as we noted in the mine section, technical problems have limited growth to-date.
